title: Researchers do not agree on what counts as joint attention
summary: A 2021 paper says one account of joint attention requires an active social check, and another counts simply looking where someone else looks.
body: Allison Gabouer and Heather Bortfeld say the field uses two broad accounts. The social account wants an active, back-and-forth coordination, including some sign that a partner noticed the shared target. The associative account treats joint attention as looking along another person's head or gaze, without assuming the infant is reasoning about that person's mind. The authors say the debate is still open. Their own coding asks for a verification cue, so this card does not pretend they are neutral, and it does not pick a winner for the field. The disagreement is about definitions, not about a child's diagnosis.

sources.title: Revisiting how we operationalize joint attention
sources.author: Allison Gabouer and Heather Bortfeld
sources.note: Supports the social versus associative accounts, the authors' statement that the debate continues, and their coding rule that verification is required. Peer-reviewed open copy.

contested_views.label: Social account
contested_views.summary: Joint attention is an active triadic coordination, and a qualifying episode includes a sign that one partner has noticed the other's attention.

contested_views.label: Associative account
contested_views.summary: Joint attention can be two people looking at the same target because the infant follows a head turn, without a claim that the infant represents the other person's mind.
